title: Behavior of inline nonce/hash script if source text is modified between preparation and evaluation
body:
For an inline script element, it looks like nonce & hash checks occur during “prepare a script” based on the text content of the element at that time. However even with synchronous scripts, the text content may be mutated prior to evaluation and I was surprised to not find anything in the spec that would invalidate a prior successful check if this occurs.

Script preparation, queuing, and readiness are very complex so I could easily be missing something. However this example document did evaluate the “nonce-b” script with code seemingly injected after preparation in both Chromium and FF:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>

<meta http-equiv="content-security-policy" content="script-src
  'nonce-a'
  'nonce-b'
  'sha256-W2eTK4ZUkcQqk5mrz9+lRNMr07A0NhaJbqUrIs9K8WI='
">

<script nonce="a">
  new MutationObserver(records => records
    .filter(record => record.target.localName === "script")
    .flatMap(record => [ ...record.addedNodes ])
    .filter(node => node.nodeType === 3)
    .forEach(text => {
      text.insertData(0, "console.group('inject!');")
      text.appendData(";console.groupEnd();");
    })
  ).observe(document, {
    childList: true,
    characterData: true,
    subtree: true
  });
</script>

<script nonce="b">console.log("nonced");</script>
<script>console.log("hashed");</script>
```

Behavior for the hash script was inconsistent, though: Chromium rejected the injected hashed script, while FF did evaluate it with the modifications.

Chromium:
![Edge console printing the injection-wrapped output for the nonced script but not the hashed script](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6257356/166326274-6bce4434-64ea-4e9a-9b47-9d023ea3fc08.png)

FF:
![Firefox console printing the injection-wrapped output](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6257356/166326138-c69e172e-a332-4830-9b5e-5744ed1d8e05.png)

Which (if either) of these behaviors is what’s specified? And more broadly: if the algorithms for determining whether these scripts are permitted to run take the source text as an argument, shouldn’t they occur at a juncture where further modification of that source text is no longer possible?
